content.prompt: A bag contains 1000 balls, some of which are red, some blue and the rest yellow. The probability of drawing a red ball is $\frac{1}{25}$ and the probability of drawing a yellow ball is $\frac{7}{20}$. Find:

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\text{Number of yellow balls}&=\frac{7}{20}\times1000\\\text{Number of yellow balls}&=350\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\text{Number of red balls}&=\frac{1}{25}\times1000\\\text{Number of red balls}&=40\\\text{Number of blue balls}&=1000-350-40\\\text{Number of blue balls}&=610\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: the number of yellow balls that need to be removed to make the probability of drawing a red ball $\frac{1}{20}$

answer.short:
200 yellow balls.

The 40 red balls remain, so the new total must be 800.
answer.worked:
There are $\frac{1}{25}\times1000=40$ red balls. Let $x$ be the number of yellow balls removed. The red count stays 40 and the total becomes $1000-x$.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{40}{1000-x}&=\frac{1}{20}\\1000-x&=800\\x&=200\end{align*}$$

Remove 200 yellow balls. Check: $\frac{40}{1000-200}=\frac{1}{20}$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: the number of yellow balls (from the original 1000) that need to be removed so that the probability of drawing a yellow ball is $\frac{1}{6}$

answer.short:
220 yellow balls.

Removing yellow balls reduces both the yellow count and the total.
answer.worked:
Start with the original 350 yellow balls and 1000 balls altogether. Let $x$ be the number of yellow balls removed.

$$\begin{align*}\frac{350-x}{1000-x}&=\frac{1}{6}\\6(350-x)&=1000-x\\2100-6x&=1000-x\\1100&=5x\\x&=220\end{align*}$$

Remove 220 yellow balls. Check: $\frac{350-220}{1000-220}=\frac{130}{780}=\frac{1}{6}$.

content.prompt: A box contains 3 black and 1 yellow ball. A second box contains 2 black and 2 yellow balls. A ball is taken from the first box and put in the second. A ball is then withdrawn from the second box. Find the probability that the ball taken from the second box is:

answer.short:
$\frac{11}{20}$

Label the balls and count 11 black outcomes among 20 equally likely transfer-and-draw outcomes.
answer.worked:
Label the first box's balls $B_1,B_2,B_3,Y$. Label the second box's four original balls $b_1,b_2,y_1,y_2$, and call the transferred ball $t$.

Record each outcome as (transferred ball, ball drawn). Each of the four equally likely transfers has five equally likely draws: $b_1,b_2,y_1,y_2,t$. Thus there are 20 equally likely outcomes.

The outcomes giving a black draw are:
$$\begin{gathered}(B_1,b_1),\ (B_1,b_2),\ (B_1,t),\\(B_2,b_1),\ (B_2,b_2),\ (B_2,t),\\(B_3,b_1),\ (B_3,b_2),\ (B_3,t),\\(Y,b_1),\ (Y,b_2).
\end{gathered}$$
There are 11 favourable outcomes out of 20.
$$P(\text{black from second box})=\frac{11}{20}$$

Black and yellow are complementary outcomes.

$$\begin{align*}P(\text{yellow from second box})&=1-P(\text{black from second box})\\P(\text{yellow from second box})&=1-\frac{11}{20}\\P(\text{yellow from second box})&=\frac9{20}\end{align*}$$

children.label: a

answer.short:
$\xi=\{100,101,\ldots,999\}$ and $|\xi|=900$.

The diagram shows the number of outcomes in each region.
answer.worked:
There are $999-100+1=900$ equally likely outcomes. Let $T$, $F$ and $S$ contain the numbers divisible by 3, 5 and 7 respectively.

Count multiples from the first to the last in the sample space:
$$\begin{align*}|T|&=333-34+1=300\\|F|&=199-20+1=180\\|S|&=142-15+1=128\\|T\cap F|&=66-7+1=60\\|T\cap S|&=47-5+1=43\\|F\cap S|&=28-3+1=26\\|T\cap F\cap S|&=9-1+1=9\end{align*}$$
Fill the triple intersection first, then the pair-only regions:
$$\begin{align*}|T\cap F\cap S'|&=60-9=51\\|T\cap S\cap F'|&=43-9=34\\|F\cap S\cap T'|&=26-9=17\end{align*}$$
The single-set regions are:
$$\begin{align*}|T\cap F'\cap S'|&=300-51-34-9=206\\|F\cap T'\cap S'|&=180-51-17-9=103\\|S\cap T'\cap F'|&=128-34-17-9=68\end{align*}$$
The union contains $206+103+68+51+34+17+9=488$ outcomes, leaving $900-488=412$ outside all three sets.

answer.worked:
There are $999-100+1=900$ three-digit numbers. The multiples are $100,105,\ldots,995$.

There are 900 three-digit numbers. The multiples are $105,120,\ldots,990$.

$$\begin{align*}N_{15}&=\frac{990-105}{15}+1\\N_{15}&=60\\P(15\text{ divides})&=\frac{60}{900}=\frac1{15}\end{align*}$$

$\frac7{15}$

content.prompt: Jim has $\$512$ and plays a game in which he has an equal chance of winning or losing. He wins four times and loses four times in random order. He bets half the money he has left at each stage. On a win, his stake is returned and he receives net winnings of twice his stake. On a loss, he loses his stake. How much does Jim have at the end?

answer.short:
$\$512$

Interpreting the payout as net winnings of twice the stake, each win doubles the balance and each loss halves it.
answer.worked:
Interpret “a win gives him twice what he bets” as net winnings of twice the stake, with the stake also returned. If his current balance is $M$, his stake is $\frac M2$.

$$\begin{align*}M_{\text{after a win}}&=M+2\left(\frac M2\right)\\M_{\text{after a win}}&=2M\\M_{\text{after a loss}}&=M-\frac M2\\M_{\text{after a loss}}&=\frac M2\end{align*}$$

Four wins and four losses therefore give:

$$\begin{align*}M_{\text{final}}&=512\times2^4\times\left(\frac12\right)^4\\M_{\text{final}}&=512.\end{align*}$$

The order does not matter because the same multipliers are multiplied together. Jim finishes with $\$512$.

content.prompt: In a school of 650 everybody studies French ($F$), German ($G$) or Indonesian ($I$). All but 41 study French, 12 study French and Indonesian but not German. Thirteen study Indonesian and German but not French and the same number study German only. Twice as many study French and German but not Indonesian as study all three. answer.short:

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the number studying all three languages. Then $2x$ study French and German but not Indonesian, so $3x$ study both French and German in total. Thus $3x$ also study Indonesian only.

$$\begin{align*}n(\text{French only})&=609-12-10-5\\n(\text{French only})&=582\\P(\text{French only})&=\frac{582}{650}\\P(\text{French only})&=\frac{291}{325}.\end{align*}$$

The 28 students in a class all buy music CDs. The categories they choose are rock ($R$), folk ($F$) and classical ($C$). One student buys classical CDs only. Nine students buy folk CDs only and five students buy rock CDs only. Also,
$$|R\cap C|=12,\quad |C\cap F\cap R|=|F^{\mathrm c}|\quad\text{and}\quad |F\cap R|>|F\cap C|.$$

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the number in all three sets, $y$ the number in classical and folk only, and $z$ the number in folk and rock only. The classical-and-rock-only region contains $12-x$ students. Since everyone buys at least one category, the outside region contains 0.

The students outside $F$ are in classical only, rock only, or classical and rock only:
$$\begin{align*}x&=1+5+(12-x)\\2x&=18\\x&=9.\end{align*}$$
The seven disjoint regions total 28:
$$\begin{align*}28&=1+9+5+(12-9)+9+y+z\\y+z&=1.\end{align*}$$
The inequality $|F\cap R|>|F\cap C|$ gives $9+z>9+y$, so $z>y$. As region counts are non-negative integers, $y=0$ and $z=1$.
$$\begin{align*}|C\cap F|&=9+0\\|C\cap F|&=9\\P(C\cap F)&=\frac{9}{28}.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Weather records for July 2010 in Sydney showed that the month had no hot, calm, dry days. Of the 31 days, 7 were wet and cold but not windy, 4 were wet and windy but not cold, 8 were cold and windy but dry. 16 days were windy, 22 were cold and 2 were wet but not cold or windy. If a day is chosen at random. What is the probability that the day was:

answer.short:
$\dfrac{1}{31}$.

Exactly one day lies in all three weather sets.
answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the number of cold, wet and windy days. In a three-set Venn diagram, wet only is 2, wet-and-cold only is 7, wet-and-windy only is 4, and cold-and-windy only is 8. The outside region is 0.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Cold only}&=22-7-8-x\\\text{Cold only}&=7-x\\\text{Windy only}&=16-4-8-x\\\text{Windy only}&=4-x.\end{align*}$$
Summing the disjoint regions:
$$\begin{align*}31&=2+7+4+8+x+(7-x)+(4-x)\\31&=32-x\\x&=1\\P(\text{cold, wet and windy})&=\frac{1}{31}.\end{align*}$$

The cold-only region is $7-x$. From part a, $x=1$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Cold, calm and dry days}&=7-1\\\text{Cold, calm and dry days}&=6\\P(\text{cold but calm and dry})&=\frac{6}{31}.\end{align*}$$

entries.description:
There are many situations in which it would be useful to be able to measure how likely (or unlikely) it is that an event will occur. We can do this in mathematics by using the idea of probability, which we define as a number between 0 and 1 that we assign to any event we are interested in. Then:
• a probability of 1 represents an event that is ‘certain’ or ‘guaranteed to happen’
• a probability of 0 represents an event that we would describe as ‘impossible’ or one that ‘cannot possibly occur’
• an event that has a probability 1/2 is as likely to occur as not to occur
• an event that has a probability close to 0 is unlikely to occur
• an event that has a probability close to 1 is likely to occur.
In this chapter we look at methods for determining probabilities.

The probability of the event A is written P(A).
Probabilities are assigned to events in such a way that:
0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1 for all events A
That is, the probability of an event is a number between 0 and 1 inclusive.

probability of an event = (number of outcomes favourable to that event)/(total number of outcomes)

entries.description:
The complement of an event
Sometimes, rather than being interested in seeing if the event A happens, we are interested in the event ‘not A’. For instance, we might want to know the probability that it does not rain tomorrow, or that a particular team does not win a premiership, or that the number 40 is not drawn out in a lottery draw.
